snapshots.title: The route and the shortcut
snapshots.alt: Nadia asks how far Eli is from his start. The notebook shows three meters east followed by four meters north, a seven-meter walking route. The straight displacement still needs to be found.
snapshots.body: The novel walks 3 m east, then 4 m north. The preceding slide swaps those two legs.
snapshots.question: Which results stay the same when the legs swap? Which direction changes?
snapshots.work: Part 1 · Check the route and resultant

snapshots.title: The resultant has a direction
snapshots.alt: A schematic triangle joins a three-meter east arrow to a four-meter north arrow. The resultant runs from the first tail to the final tip. Its magnitude is five meters and its direction is 53.1 degrees north of east.
snapshots.body: Translate an arrow without turning or stretching it. Use a stated scale for your own drawing.
snapshots.question: How would a rotated or stretched arrow change the result?
snapshots.work: Part 1 · Check the route and resultant

snapshots.title: Rebuild the fictional velocity
snapshots.alt: The classroom model points positive x away from Earth. The velocity components are negative 8210 meters per second in x and positive 2200 in y. They give speed about 8500 meters per second and direction about 15 degrees from toward Earth toward positive y.
snapshots.body: With +x away from Earth, vₓ = −8,210 m/s and vᵧ = +2,200 m/s.
snapshots.question: Why is the direction about 165° from +x, rather than 15° from +x?

snapshots.title: Check the angle before choosing sine or cosine
snapshots.alt: The same ten-meter-per-second vector is shown 30 degrees above horizontal, equivalently 60 degrees from vertical. Its components stay 8.66 horizontally and 5 vertically. Mr. Antocci explains that cosine belongs to the component beside the marked angle.
snapshots.body: Changing the reference angle does not change the arrow. Cosine goes with the adjacent component.
snapshots.question: How can both angle descriptions produce the same two components?
